query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 under elevated-temperature oxidizing or reducing conditions is governed mainly by the nature and stability of the surface oxide layer. In this alloy, the synergistic interaction among Al, Ti, and Cr controls the formation of mixed oxide films—where increased Al favors a dense, protective alumina (or mixed Al/Cr oxide) layer while Ti and Cr adjust the nucleation and growth kinetics. Systematic compositional adjustments are expected to shift the balance between forming a protective versus a non-protective oxide, ultimately dictating the degradation rate without altering the bulk FCC matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy with the nominal composition Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 that exhibits homogeneous elemental distribution and high strength/fatigue properties.
generation.intervention: Systematically adjust the relative concentrations of Al, Ti, and Cr (using a NICE-inspired mapping approach) to decouple their individual contributions to surface oxide formation under high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Isothermal exposure at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800°C and 1200°C) in controlled gas atmospheres: one oxidizing (with a defined O2 content) and one reducing (such as H2-rich or CO-containing environment), ensuring that the thermal history and processing conditions remain constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The composition, morphology, and stability of the surface oxide layer which forms as a result of the preferential oxidation of Al (and modified by Ti and Cr), while leaving the bulk FCC microstructure intact.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature exposure, the elemental affinities drive selective oxidation: Al tends to form protective alumina, whereas Ti and Cr adjust the kinetics and structure of the oxide layer. These synergistic interactions control whether the oxide film is continuous and dense (minimizing further oxidation and degradation) or porous and non-protective. In oxidizing environments, an optimized balance promotes formation of a protective film; in reducing environments, instability or partial reduction of the oxide may accelerate degradation. The systematic compositional changes allow the decoupling of these effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy variants with increased Al (or an optimized Al/Ti/Cr ratio) will develop a more uniform, dense, and protective oxide layer under oxidizing conditions, resulting in lower weight gain and less mechanical degradation compared to the baseline alloy. Conversely, compositions with reduced Al or excessive Ti may form less protective, more porous oxide films, leading to accelerated degradation. Similar trends are expected under reducing conditions where oxide reduction dynamics further influence surface integrity.
generation.baseline: The starting-state Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy shows a moderate degree of degradation due to formation of a mixed oxide film under high-temperature exposure, reflecting the net synergistic effects of its constituent elements.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable in the high-temperature regime typical of turbine or related applications (approximately 800°C to 1200°C) under controlled oxidizing or reducing atmospheres. It assumes that the FCC matrix remains stable and that compositional variations do not induce unwanted phase separation.
generation.uncertainty: While the overall role of Al in forming protective oxides is well documented, the precise quantitative contributions of Ti and Cr to the oxide film’s structure and stability remain uncertain. The balance between beneficial oxide formation and degradation under reducing environments also has inherent uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloy variants with systematic compositional modifications in Al, Ti, and Cr (e.g., ±10–20% relative to the baseline composition) while ensuring retention of a single FCC phase. Subject these samples to prolonged isothermal exposures at 800°C and 1200°C in both an oxidizing atmosphere (with controlled O2 levels) and a reducing atmosphere (e.g., H2-rich). Characterize the surface oxide composition, morphology, and thickness (using techniques like XPS, SEM, and AFM), measure weight changes via thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and assess changes in mechanical properties.
measurements: Degradation of mechanical properties (tensile or fatigue testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the systematic changes in the elemental composition do not produce corresponding, predictable variations in the surface oxide characteristics (i.e., if increased Al does not lead to a denser oxide film and improved degradation resistance, or if reducing atmospheres do not consistently alter the oxide stability relative to the compositional changes), then the hypothesis that the degradation mechanism is predominantly controlled by the synergistic oxide formation mediated by Al, Ti, and Cr is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It is not possible to identify the mechanism(s) responsible for the Sn effect on oxidation because all the research is on Nb-silicide-based alloys with solute additions of Al, Cr, Si, and Ti and other transition, refractory, simple metal, and metalloid additions plus Sn. For example, the two patents by Jackson et al. [,] are for multi-element alloys with solute additions that include Hf, one or more of the refractory metals Mo, Ta, and W, the simple metals, Sn and B, and metalloid element Ge. The alloys studied by Tsakiropoulos and co-workers include Hf, Mo, and Sn [] or Fe, Hf, V, and Sn []. Knittel et al. [] studied MASC type alloys with Hf and different Sn concentrations but with no additions of Ge and B (the MASC alloy nominal composition (at.%) is Nb-25Ti-16Si-8Hf-2Al-2Cr).

Considering that Hf, Si, Sn, and Ti are key elements for oxidation resistance and that refractory metals, in particular Mo and W, are key for strength and creep [,,,,], the synergy of Hf, Sn, and Ti that promotes Ti rich Nbss (i) improves the oxidation resistance of the Nbss but (ii) reduces the strength and creep of the Nbss in alloys with RM addition, owing to the relationship between the concentration of Ti and RMs in the Nbss in RM(Nb)ICs and RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs (e.g., see Figure S4 in the Supplemental Data in [], Figure 12 in [], and Figure 12 in []). Thus, a challenge for alloy design is to “balance” these effects. This is achievable with the alloy design methodology NICE [,,].

reading.lever: Apply systematic compositional adjustments based on NICE-inspired mapping to decouple individual elemental contributions to surface oxide behavior.
reading.why: Leveraging insights from Nb‐silicide studies, this approach can isolate synergistic effects in the additively manufactured HEA without altering its bulk fcc integrity.
